lessons.title: Translations and mirrors
lessons.summary: Find image coordinates and explain how translations and reflections preserve size.
lessons.objective: Find image coordinates and explain how translations and reflections preserve size.
lessons.before: A translation slides every point the same way.
lessons.ideas:
For a column vector, the top entry gives the signed horizontal move and the bottom entry gives the signed vertical move. Add these entries to the corresponding coordinates.

For a vertical or horizontal mirror, change only the coordinate across the line. For y = x, swap coordinates. For y = −x, swap and negate both coordinates.

When the two points differ, their perpendicular bisector is the mirror line. Check a second matching pair if you have one.
lessons.method:
Check several vertices, using the same vector each time.

Check the mirror line is halfway between the point and its image.

Give an equation for the line when using coordinates.
mistakes: A negative horizontal number means move left. A negative vertical number means move down.
A point on the mirror stays fixed.
A line through both points is not the perpendicular bisector.

examples.title: Translate a point and preserve its distances
examples.question:
Point A is \((-5,-6)\). Its translation vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Give the coordinates of the image of A.

    [2]

  2. A whole triangle is moved by this vector. Why is it congruent to its image?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The upper entry moves x right by 2. The lower entry moves y down by 3.

Add each signed entry to its own coordinate.

\((-3,-9)\)

(b) The whole figure slides. It does not stretch or rotate.

Every vertex moves the same way, so side lengths and angle sizes stay unchanged.

examples.title: Reflect a point in a named line
examples.question:
Point A has coordinates \((6,-4)\). The mirror line is \(x=1\).

  1. Give the image coordinates.

    [2]

  2. Describe a geometric way to check your image.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Keep the y-coordinate. Go the same horizontal distance to the opposite side of x = 1.

\((-4,-4)\)

(b) A point on the mirror is unchanged. Other points cross to the opposite side at the same perpendicular distance.

The segment joining the point and its image has the mirror line as its perpendicular bisector, unless the point is on the mirror.

examples.title: Recover the mirror line
examples.question:
A point \((-6,-6)\) has image \((12,-6)\) after a reflection in a vertical line.

  1. The mirror line has equation x = k. Find k.

    [2]

  2. Explain why this is a line rather than just a point.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The perpendicular segment between the two points is horizontal. Its midpoint has x-coordinate half of -6 + 12.

\(3\)

(b) All points on that vertical line are equidistant from the point and its image.

The mirror is the perpendicular bisector of the two points. It is the entire vertical line through the midpoint.

lessons.title: Rotations and enlargements
lessons.summary: Use centres, directions and angle sizes for turns, and whole-number scale factors for enlargements.
lessons.objective: Use centres, directions and angle sizes for turns, and whole-number scale factors for enlargements.
lessons.before: A rotation needs a centre, a direction and an angle.
lessons.ideas:
Think about the displacement from the centre. For a 90° clockwise turn, right becomes down and up becomes right. For 90° anticlockwise, right becomes up and up becomes left. A 180° turn reverses both moves.

Draw a ray from the centre through a vertex. Multiply the distance from the centre by the same positive scale factor along each ray. A point at the centre stays fixed.

For a pair away from the centre, compare image distance with original distance. If the centre is unknown, draw two non-parallel lines joining two pairs and use their crossing.
lessons.method:
Label the centre before making the turn.

Check the shape remains similar and the matching sides use the same factor.

State the centre as well as the scale factor when identifying an enlargement.
mistakes: Rotating about the origin only works when that is the stated centre.
Multiplying the coordinates directly only works for an origin centre.
Compare both distances from the same centre.

examples.title: Turn a point around a fixed centre
examples.question:
Point P is \((0,-1)\). Rotate it 90° clockwise about \((-1,-3)\).

  1. Give the image coordinates.

    [2]

  2. State which point is unchanged by the turn.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Measure P from the centre first. It is 1 right and 2 up.

Turn that displacement 90° clockwise to get \((2,-1)\). Then add the centre coordinates.

\((1,-4)\)

(b) A rotation keeps its own centre fixed.

\((-1,-3)\)

examples.title: Scale a point from an enlargement centre
examples.question:
Enlarge a figure by scale factor 2 with centre \((-3,-2)\). Its vertex P is \((-2,0)\).

  1. Find the image coordinates of P.

    [2]

  2. A side is 7 cm long on the original. Find its new length and say what happens to its angles.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Start at the centre and move 1 across and 2 up to reach P. Make both movements 2 times as large.

Add the new displacement to the centre.

\((-1,2)\)

(b) Lengths multiply by the scale factor. The shape keeps its angles.

14 cm. Angle sizes are unchanged.

examples.title: Identify the integer scale of an enlargement
examples.question:
An enlargement of centre \((-1,2)\) takes P \((7,6)\) to P′ \((15,10)\).

  1. Find the scale factor.

    [2]

  2. How can you use a straightedge to check the given centre?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The old horizontal displacement from the centre is 8. The new horizontal displacement is 16.

The vertical displacements scale from 4 to 8, confirming the same factor.

\(2\)

(b) Repeat for another pair of matching points to locate the centre if it is unknown.

The original point, its image and the centre should lie on the same line.
